## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand the difference between opening a file and opening a folder in VS Code — and why opening a folder is almost always what you want to do.

You'll also open your actual course project folder so VS Code knows the context of your work.

## Files vs Folders: Why It Matters

Most text editors work with one file at a time. You open a file, edit it, save it, done. VS Code *can* work this way — but that's not how it's designed.

VS Code is designed to work with **folders** (also called workspaces). When you open a folder, VS Code can:
- Show you all files and subfolders in the Explorer panel
- Search text across every file in the folder at once
- Run Git commands on the entire project
- Let AI tools like GitHub Copilot understand the full context of your project
- Run the integrated terminal starting at the right location

Here's the key distinction:

- **File > Open File** — opens a single file. VS Code has no awareness of any other files around it. The Explorer panel stays empty.
- **File > Open Folder** — opens an entire folder. VS Code treats that folder as your project. The Explorer panel fills with your files. This is almost always what you want.

Think of it this way: opening a file is like handing someone a single page from a book. Opening a folder is like handing them the whole book — they can understand the full context.

**Quick shortcut: `code .`**
If you have a terminal open and you're in the folder you want to work in, you can type `code .` and press Enter. VS Code opens that folder instantly. The `.` means "current directory." This only works if you checked "Add to PATH" during installation (lesson 5-2).

## What is a Workspace?

You'll hear the word "workspace" used in two slightly different ways:

1. **Informally** — just the folder you currently have open in VS Code. Most of the time this is what people mean.

2. **VS Code Multi-root Workspace** — a special `.code-workspace` file that lets you add multiple separate folders to VS Code at the same time. For example, you might have a front-end folder and a back-end folder open simultaneously, each showing in the Explorer sidebar.

For this course, we're only using the simple version: one folder open at a time. You don't need multi-root workspaces right now.

**Trust prompt:** The first time you open a folder, VS Code may ask: *"Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?"* Click **Yes, I trust the authors**. VS Code asks this as a safety measure — on a folder full of your own files, always click Yes.

## How to Open a Folder

**Method 1 — From the menu:**
1. Click **File** in the menu bar
2. Click **Open Folder...**
3. A file browser window opens
4. Navigate to the folder you want to open
5. Click **Select Folder** (Windows) or **Open** (Mac)

**Method 2 — Drag and drop:**
Drag a folder from File Explorer directly onto the VS Code window. VS Code opens it.

**Method 3 — From the terminal:**
1. Open any terminal (PowerShell, Command Prompt, or VS Code's integrated terminal)
2. Navigate to the folder using `cd`
3. Type `code .` and press Enter

**Method 4 — Recent folders:**
File > Open Recent shows folders you've opened before. Click any of them to reopen quickly.

All four methods do the same thing.

sections.title: Open Your Course Project
sections.content:
You created the `ai-course-projects` folder in lesson 4.2. Now open it as a workspace in VS Code.

**Step 1 — Open the folder:**
1. In VS Code, click **File** in the menu bar
2. Click **Open Folder...**
3. In the file browser, navigate to: `C:\Users\[YourName]\Documents\ai-course-projects`
   (Replace `[YourName]` with your actual Windows username — the name you see in File Explorer under C:\Users)
4. Click **Select Folder**
5. If VS Code asks about trusting the folder → click **Yes, I trust the authors**

**Step 2 — Confirm it worked:**
- [ ] The Explorer panel on the left shows your folder structure
- [ ] You can see the `exercises`, `notes`, and `prompts` subfolders
- [ ] Click `exercises` to expand it — `hello.html` from lesson 4.6 should be there
- [ ] Click `hello.html` — it opens in the Editor Area
- [ ] Look at the Status Bar at the bottom — confirm it shows `HTML` as the language mode

**Step 3 — Try `code .` (optional, confirms PATH is set up):**
1. Press Ctrl+` to open the integrated terminal inside VS Code
2. The terminal should already be pointing at your `ai-course-projects` folder
3. Type `pwd` to confirm your location
4. Type `ls` to see the folder contents listed

If the terminal shows the right folder, your PATH setup from the installer is working correctly.

This folder — `ai-course-projects` — is your workspace for the rest of Part 5 and beyond.

**You've completed lesson 5-4.** VS Code is now open with your course project folder. The Explorer panel shows your files, and VS Code understands the full context of your project. Next: creating and managing files without ever leaving VS Code.
